system.description:
Petits-Nains — Noegyth Nibin

Les Petits-Nains, appelés Noegyth Nibin en sindarin, forment une branche ancienne, déchue et presque éteinte des Khazâd. Bien avant le lever du Soleil et de la Lune, ils vivaient déjà dans des demeures secrètes et dispersées. Mîm est leur représentant le plus célèbre, mais quelques familles auraient survécu à la submersion du Beleriand.

Ils ne sont ni une Race entièrement étrangère aux Khazâd ni une simple Culture régionale. Leur longue séparation, les persécutions, l’endogamie et les privations ont transformé leur apparence et leur mode de vie.

Origines et exil

Ils descendraient d’un groupe de bannis de Nogrod, exilé après un meurtre. L’éloignement des grandes Maisons entraîna la perte de traditions artisanales, l’isolement des familles, une défiance croissante et une adaptation à une existence clandestine fondée sur la cueillette, les herbes et la dissimulation.

Les premiers habitants du Beleriand

Ils occupèrent plusieurs régions du Beleriand avant l’arrivée des Elfes. Certains furent chassés, traqués ou tués, ce qui nourrit leur haine durable envers les Elfes, particulièrement les Noldor. Leur mémoire conserve le souvenir de cavernes confisquées, de familles disparues et de terres perdues.

Amon Rûdh et Mîm

Mîm vivait avec ses fils dans les cavernes d’Amon Rûdh. Son histoire illustre leur attachement farouche au foyer, leur haine des Orcs, leur ressentiment envers les Elfes et leur volonté de survivre. Il ne doit toutefois pas être considéré comme le modèle moral de tout son peuple.

Un peuple presque éteint

Leurs communautés ne comptent souvent que quelques familles, un unique clan ou plusieurs survivants vivant dans un réseau de cavernes. Révéler l’emplacement d’une demeure pourrait condamner tout le groupe, ce qui explique leur secret extrême.

Apparence

Ils mesurent généralement entre 90 cm et 1,20 m. Leur peau va du brun sombre au gris, leur teint est souvent rougeaud, leurs membres noueux, leur tête large, leurs épaules courbées et leur barbe fine, broussailleuse et rarement entretenue.

Leur apparence peut être expliquée par la malnutrition, les conditions de vie difficiles et l’adaptation aux passages étroits, plutôt que par une corruption morale inhérente.

Longévité et endurance

Ils vivent généralement entre 250 et 400 ans. Malgré leur petite taille et leur posture voûtée, ils possèdent une endurance remarquable, adaptée aux déplacements souterrains, aux marches nocturnes, au transport de provisions et aux périodes de rationnement.

Résistances et vision

Comme les autres Khazâd, ils résistent bien au feu et au froid. Ils voient très bien dans la pénombre et sont parfaitement adaptés aux cavernes, tunnels, ruines et forêts nocturnes.

Furtivité

Leur petite taille et leur longue habitude de la clandestinité en font d’excellents infiltrateurs. Ils apprennent à marcher sans bruit, cacher une entrée, effacer des traces, se glisser dans des passages étroits, observer sans être vus et créer de fausses pistes.

Demeures cachées

Ils vivent dans des habitats creusés dans les collines, falaises ou affleurements rocheux. Une demeure comprend généralement une entrée dissimulée, des couloirs sinueux, une salle commune, quelques cellules familiales, un garde-manger, un atelier, une petite forge et plusieurs galeries de fuite.

Cueillette et nature

Moins compétents que les grandes Maisons dans les arts de la forge et de la maçonnerie, ils sont meilleurs dans l’usage des herbes, des racines, des champignons, des poisons et des ressources forestières. Leur rapport à la nature est utilitaire mais souvent respectueux, car une forêt généreuse assure la survie du clan.

Artisanat

Ils pratiquent forge simple, coutellerie, petite orfèvrerie, empennage, pièges, taille de pierre, bois, cuir et préparation d’herbes. Leurs objets paraissent souvent grossiers mais peuvent cacher mécanismes ingénieux, caches, lames escamotables ou poisons.

Vêtements

Ils portent des vêtements sombres et épais : capuches couvrant le visage, lourdes capes, bottes de cuir, pourpoints et pantalons ajustés. Les objets précieux sont dissimulés sous les vêtements ou cachés dans les demeures.

Société et famille

Leur société est fondée sur la famille et la survie immédiate. L’autorité appartient au plus ancien, au propriétaire de la demeure, au meilleur chasseur ou à l’artisan le plus compétent. Le mariage est monogame, et les enfants sont extrêmement précieux en raison de la faiblesse démographique.

Tempérament

Ils sont silencieux, possessifs, soupçonneux et rusés. Ces traits doivent être compris comme les conséquences d’une longue histoire de persécution. Ils peuvent être loyaux envers leur famille, reconnaissants envers un véritable ami et généreux lorsqu’ils ne se sentent pas menacés.

Religion

Ils révèrent Aulë sous une forme isolée de son nom et honorent aussi Yavanna, car les plantes et la forêt sont essentielles à leur survie. Leurs rites associent pierre, métal, cavernes, subsistance, mémoire des ancêtres et protection des familles.

Langues

Ils parlent surtout le westron et parfois le sindarin à l’extérieur. Entre eux, ils utilisent une forme archaïque et particulière du khuzdul, riche en termes liés aux anciennes demeures et à la forêt.

Relations

Leurs relations avec les Khazâd sont complexes : parenté reconnue mais souvenir du bannissement. Ils haïssent particulièrement les Elfes, surtout les Noldor, et combattent aussi les Orcs, Wargs, Trolls, brigands et monstres souterrains.

Armes, armures et combat

Ils utilisent cimeterres, dagues, arbalètes, frondes, épées courtes, hachettes, marteaux, lances et javelots. Le cuir souple et la maille ample sont courants.

Ils combattent par pièges, embuscades, tirs d’arbalète, fausses retraites, galeries de fuite, herbes et poisons. Dans leur propre demeure, chaque passage peut devenir une arme.

Magie et professions

De rares Mages existent parmi eux, mais plusieurs voies magiques et mentales restent interdites. Ils ne développent pas la tradition militaire disciplinée des grandes Maisons ; leurs combattants sont davantage chasseurs, roublards, gardiens ou éclaireurs.

Amon Rûdh et Mîm

Mîm, le plus célèbre des Petits-Nains, vivait avec ses fils dans les cavernes d’Amon Rûdh. Sa demeure devint un temps le refuge de Túrin et de ses compagnons. Son histoire illustre l’attachement farouche au foyer, la haine des Orcs, le ressentiment envers les Elfes, la mémoire des humiliations et la volonté de préserver les derniers membres de sa famille. Il ne doit toutefois pas être considéré comme le modèle moral de tout son peuple.

Un peuple presque éteint

Même avant leur déclin, leurs communautés restaient petites et séparées. Au Troisième Âge, un groupe peut ne comprendre que quelques familles apparentées, un unique clan, plusieurs individus vivant dans un réseau de cavernes ou des survivants dispersés ignorant l’existence des autres. Cette rareté explique leur caractère extrêmement secret : révéler l’emplacement d’une demeure pourrait condamner toute la communauté.

Cueillette et connaissance de la nature

Les Petits-Nains possèdent moins de compétences en forge et en maçonnerie que les grandes Maisons, mais sont bien meilleurs dans l’usage des herbes, la cueillette et la connaissance du monde naturel. Ils savent reconnaître plantes comestibles, racines nutritives, herbes médicinales, poisons, champignons, traces animales, changements de saison et refuges naturels. Leur rapport à la nature est plus utilitaire que celui des Elfes, mais peut devenir profondément respectueux.

Société, propriété et famille

Leur société est fondée sur la famille et la survie immédiate du groupe. La possession joue un rôle central : chaque outil, réserve et cache peut déterminer la survie de tous. Le mariage est monogame et dure toute la vie ; les enfants sont extrêmement précieux en raison de la faiblesse démographique. Ils apprennent très tôt à rester silencieux, reconnaître les plantes, cacher les traces, ne jamais révéler la demeure et mémoriser les itinéraires de fuite.

Une morale façonnée par la persécution

Les récits anciens les décrivent comme silencieux, possessifs, cupides, soupçonneux et parfois traîtres. Pour une représentation plus nuancée, ces traits doivent être compris comme les conséquences d’une longue histoire de persécution : le silence protège les demeures, la possessivité protège des ressources rares, la ruse compense l’infériorité numérique et un accord imposé sous la menace n’est pas considéré comme légitime. Cela n’empêche pas une loyauté profonde envers la famille ou un véritable ami.

La Race Petits-Nains — Noegyth Nibin convient surtout au Premier Âge, puis à de rares survivants des Âges suivants. Elle doit rester Restreinte. Petty-dwarves — Noegyth Nibin

The Petty-dwarves, called Noegyth Nibin in Sindarin, form an ancient, fallen and nearly extinct branch of the Khazâd. Long before the rising of the Sun and Moon, they already lived in secret and scattered dwellings. Mîm is their most famous representative, but a few families may have survived the drowning of Beleriand.

They are neither a Race entirely separate from the Khazâd nor merely a regional Culture. Their long separation, persecution, inbreeding and deprivation transformed both their appearance and way of life.

Origins and exile

They are said to descend from a group of exiles from Nogrod, banished after a murder. Separation from the great Houses led to the loss of craft traditions, the isolation of families, growing distrust and adaptation to a clandestine existence based on gathering, herbs and concealment.

The first inhabitants of Beleriand

They occupied several regions of Beleriand before the arrival of the Elves. Some were driven out, hunted or killed, feeding their lasting hatred of the Elves, especially the Noldor. Their memory preserves the loss of caves, vanished families and stolen lands.

Amon Rûdh and Mîm

Mîm lived with his sons in the caves of Amon Rûdh. His story illustrates their fierce attachment to home, hatred of Orcs, resentment toward Elves and determination to survive. He should not, however, be regarded as the moral model for his entire people.

A nearly extinct people

Their communities often consist of only a few families, a single clan or several survivors living within a network of caves. Revealing the location of a dwelling could doom the entire group, explaining their extreme secrecy.

Appearance

They generally stand between 90 cm and 1.20 m tall. Their skin ranges from dark brown to grey, their complexion is often ruddy, their limbs knotted, their heads broad, shoulders hunched and beards thin, bushy and seldom groomed.

Their appearance can be explained by malnutrition, harsh living conditions and adaptation to narrow passages rather than by any inherent moral corruption.

Longevity and endurance

They generally live between 250 and 400 years. Despite their small stature and stooped posture, they possess remarkable endurance suited to underground travel, night marches, carrying provisions and periods of rationing.

Resistances and vision

Like other Khazâd, they resist fire and cold well. They see very well in dim light and are perfectly adapted to caverns, tunnels, ruins and forests by night.

Stealth

Their small size and long habit of clandestine life make them excellent infiltrators. They learn to walk silently, conceal an entrance, erase tracks, slip through narrow passages, observe without being seen and lay false trails.

Hidden dwellings

They live in homes dug into hills, cliffs or rocky outcrops. A dwelling usually includes a concealed entrance, winding corridors, a common room, a few family cells, a pantry, a workshop, a small forge and several escape tunnels.

Gathering and nature

Less skilled than the great Houses in smithcraft and masonry, they are better at the use of herbs, roots, fungi, poisons and woodland resources. Their relationship with nature is practical but often respectful, because a generous forest ensures the clan's survival.

Craftsmanship

They practise simple smithing, knifemaking, minor jewellery, fletching, trapmaking, stonework, woodworking, leatherwork and herbal preparation. Their objects often appear crude but may conceal ingenious mechanisms, hidden compartments, retractable blades or poisons.

Clothing

They wear dark, heavy clothing: hoods covering the face, thick cloaks, leather boots, fitted doublets and trousers. Precious objects are concealed beneath clothing or hidden in their dwellings.

Society and family

Their society is founded on family and immediate survival. Authority belongs to the eldest, the owner of the dwelling, the best hunter or the most skilled craftsman. Marriage is monogamous, and children are exceedingly precious because of their low population.

Temperament

They are quiet, possessive, suspicious and cunning. These traits should be understood as consequences of a long history of persecution. They can be loyal to family, grateful to a true friend and generous when they do not feel threatened.

Religion

They revere Aulë under an isolated form of his name and also honour Yavanna, for plants and forests are essential to their survival. Their rites combine stone, metal, caverns, subsistence, remembrance of ancestors and the protection of families.

Languages

Outside their homes they chiefly speak Westron and sometimes Sindarin. Among themselves they use an archaic and distinctive form of Khuzdul, rich in terms connected with ancient dwellings and the forest.

Relations

Their relations with the Khazâd are complex: kinship is acknowledged, but so is the memory of exile. They particularly hate Elves, especially the Noldor, and also fight Orcs, Wargs, Trolls, brigands and underground monsters.

Weapons, armour and combat

They use scimitars, daggers, crossbows, slings, short swords, hatchets, hammers, spears and javelins. Supple leather and loose mail are common.

They fight through traps, ambushes, crossbow fire, feigned retreats, escape tunnels, herbs and poisons. Within their own dwelling, every passage can become a weapon.

Magic and professions

Rare Mages exist among them, but several magical and mental paths remain forbidden. They do not develop the disciplined military tradition of the great Houses; their fighters are more often hunters, rogues, guardians or scouts.

Amon Rûdh and Mîm

Mîm, the most famous of the Petty-dwarves, lived with his sons in the caves of Amon Rûdh. For a time his dwelling became a refuge for Túrin and his companions. His story illustrates fierce attachment to home, hatred of Orcs, resentment toward Elves, memory of humiliations and determination to preserve the last members of his family. He should not, however, be regarded as the moral model for his entire people.

A nearly extinct people

Even before their decline, their communities remained small and separate. By the Third Age, a group may consist of only a few related families, a single clan, several individuals living within a network of caves, or scattered survivors unaware that others still exist. This rarity explains their extreme secrecy: revealing the location of a dwelling could doom the whole community.

Gathering and knowledge of nature

Petty-dwarves possess less skill in smithing and masonry than the great Houses, but are much better at herbcraft, gathering and knowledge of the natural world. They recognise edible plants, nourishing roots, medicinal herbs, poisons, fungi, animal tracks, seasonal changes and natural shelters. Their relationship with nature is more utilitarian than that of the Elves, but can become deeply respectful.

Society, property and family

Their society is founded on family and the immediate survival of the group. Possession plays a central role: every tool, store and hiding place may determine everyone's survival. Marriage is monogamous and lasts for life; children are exceedingly precious because of the low population. They learn very early to remain silent, recognise plants, hide tracks, never reveal the dwelling and memorise escape routes.

A morality shaped by persecution

Ancient accounts describe them as quiet, possessive, greedy, suspicious and sometimes treacherous. For a more nuanced portrayal, these traits should be understood as consequences of a long history of persecution: silence protects dwellings, possessiveness protects scarce resources, cunning compensates for lack of numbers, and an agreement imposed under threat is not regarded as legitimate. None of this prevents deep loyalty to family or to a true friend.

Place in character creation

The Petty-dwarves — Noegyth Nibin Race is best suited to the First Age, and thereafter to rare survivors in later Ages. It should remain Restricted. The player should specify the location of the community, the number of survivors, the character's relationship with the Khazâd, distrust of Elves and the secret being protected.

Leurs communautés ne comptent souvent que quelques familles, un unique clan ou plusieurs survivants vivant dans un réseau de cavernes. Révéler l’emplacement d’une demeure pourrait condamner tout le groupe, ce qui explique leur secret extrême.

Apparence

Ils mesurent généralement entre 90 cm et 1,20 m. Leur peau va du brun sombre au gris, leur teint est souvent rougeaud, leurs membres noueux, leur tête large, leurs épaules courbées et leur barbe fine, broussailleuse et rarement entretenue.

Leur petite taille et leur longue habitude de la clandestinité en font d’excellents infiltrateurs. Ils apprennent à marcher sans bruit, cacher une entrée, effacer des traces, se glisser dans des passages étroits, observer sans être vus et créer de fausses pistes.

Mîm, the most famous of the Petty-dwarves, lived with his sons in the caves of Amon Rûdh. For a time his dwelling became a refuge for Túrin and his companions. He should not, however, be regarded as the moral model for his entire people.

A nearly extinct people

Even before their decline, their communities remained small and separate. By the Third Age, a group may consist of only a few related families, a single clan, several individuals living within a network of caves, or scattered survivors unaware that others still exist. This rarity explains their extreme secrecy: revealing the location of a dwelling could doom the whole community.

Gathering and knowledge of nature

Petty-dwarves possess less skill in smithing and masonry than the great Houses, but are much better at herbcraft, gathering and knowledge of the natural world. They recognise edible plants, nourishing roots, medicinal herbs, poisons, fungi, animal tracks, seasonal changes and natural shelters. Their relationship with nature is more utilitarian than that of the Elves, but can become deeply respectful.

Society, property and family

Their society is founded on family and the immediate survival of the group. Possession plays a central role: every tool, store and hiding place may determine everyone's survival. Marriage is monogamous and lasts for life; children are exceedingly precious because of the low population. They learn very early to remain silent, recognise plants, hide tracks, never reveal the dwelling and memorise escape routes.

A morality shaped by persecution

Ancient accounts describe them as quiet, possessive, greedy, suspicious and sometimes treacherous. For a more nuanced portrayal, these traits should be understood as consequences of a long history of persecution: silence protects dwellings, possessiveness protects scarce resources, cunning compensates for lack of numbers, and an agreement imposed under threat is not regarded as legitimate. None of this prevents deep loyalty to family or to a true friend.

Place in character creation

The Petty-dwarves — Noegyth Nibin Race is best suited to the First Age, and thereafter to rare survivors in later Ages. It should remain Restricted. The player should specify the location of the community, the number of survivors, the character's relationship with the Khazâd, distrust of Elves and the secret being protected.

He should not, however, be regarded as the moral model for his entire people.

A nearly extinct people

Even before their decline, their communities remained small and separate. By the Third Age, a group may consist of only a few related families, a single clan, several individuals living within a network of caves, or scattered survivors unaware that others still exist. This rarity explains their extreme secrecy: revealing the location of a dwelling could doom the whole community.

Gathering and knowledge of nature

Petty-dwarves possess less skill in smithing and masonry than the great Houses, but are much better at herbcraft, gathering and knowledge of the natural world. They recognise edible plants, nourishing roots, medicinal herbs, poisons, fungi, animal tracks, seasonal changes and natural shelters. Their relationship with nature is more utilitarian than that of the Elves, but can become deeply respectful.

Society, property and family

Their society is founded on family and the immediate survival of the group. Possession plays a central role: every tool, store and hiding place may determine everyone's survival. Marriage is monogamous and lasts for life; children are exceedingly precious because of the low population. They learn very early to remain silent, recognise plants, hide tracks, never reveal the dwelling and memorise escape routes.

A morality shaped by persecution

Ancient accounts describe them as quiet, possessive, greedy, suspicious and sometimes treacherous. For a more nuanced portrayal, these traits should be understood as consequences of a long history of persecution: silence protects dwellings, possessiveness protects scarce resources, cunning compensates for lack of numbers, and an agreement imposed under threat is not regarded as legitimate. None of this prevents deep loyalty to family or to a true friend.

The Petty-dwarves — Noegyth Nibin Race is best suited to the First Age, and thereafter to rare survivors in later Ages. It should remain Restricted. The player should specify the location of the community, the number of survivors, the character's relationship with the Khazâd, distrust of Elves and the secret being protected.

Mîm is their most famous representative, but a few families may have survived the drowning of Beleriand.

Origins and exile

Their relations with the Khazâd are complex: kinship is acknowledged, but so is the memory of exile. They particularly hate Elves, especially the Noldor, and also fight Orcs, Wargs, Trolls, brigands and underground monsters.

They use scimitars, daggers, crossbows, slings, short swords, hatchets, hammers, spears and javelins. Supple leather and loose mail are common.

They fight through traps, ambushes, crossbow fire, feigned retreats, escape tunnels, herbs and poisons. Within their own dwelling, every passage can become a weapon.

He should not, however, be regarded as the moral model for his entire people.

A nearly extinct people

Even before their decline, their communities remained small and separate. By the Third Age, a group may consist of only a few related families, a single clan, several individuals living within a network of caves, or scattered survivors unaware that others still exist. This rarity explains their extreme secrecy: revealing the location of a dwelling could doom the whole community.

Gathering and knowledge of nature

Petty-dwarves possess less skill in smithing and masonry than the great Houses, but are much better at herbcraft, gathering and knowledge of the natural world. They recognise edible plants, nourishing roots, medicinal herbs, poisons, fungi, animal tracks, seasonal changes and natural shelters. Their relationship with nature is more utilitarian than that of the Elves, but can become deeply respectful.

Society, property and family

Their society is founded on family and the immediate survival of the group. Possession plays a central role: every tool, store and hiding place may determine everyone's survival. Marriage is monogamous and lasts for life; children are exceedingly precious because of the low population. They learn very early to remain silent, recognise plants, hide tracks, never reveal the dwelling and memorise escape routes.

A morality shaped by persecution

Ancient accounts describe them as quiet, possessive, greedy, suspicious and sometimes treacherous. For a more nuanced portrayal, these traits should be understood as consequences of a long history of persecution: silence protects dwellings, possessiveness protects scarce resources, cunning compensates for lack of numbers, and an agreement imposed under threat is not regarded as legitimate. None of this prevents deep loyalty to family or to a true friend.

Place in character creation

The Petty-dwarves — Noegyth Nibin Race is best suited to the First Age, and thereafter to rare survivors in later Ages. It should remain Restricted. The player should specify the location of the community, the number of survivors, the character's relationship with the Khazâd, distrust of Elves and the secret being protected.

The Petty-dwarves — Noegyth Nibin Race is best suited to the First Age, and thereafter to rare survivors in later Ages. It should remain Restricted. The player should specify the location of the community, the number of survivors, the character's relationship with the Khazâd, distrust of Elves and the secret being protected.

The Petty-dwarves — Noegyth Nibin Race is best suited to the First Age, and thereafter to rare survivors in later Ages. It should remain Restricted. Petty-dwarves possess less skill in smithing and masonry than the great Houses, but are much better at herbcraft, gathering and knowledge of the natural world. Their society is founded on family and the immediate survival of the group. Possession plays a central role: every tool, store and hiding place may determine everyone's survival. Marriage is monogamous and lasts for life; children are exceedingly precious because of the low population. Ancient accounts describe them as quiet, possessive, greedy, suspicious and sometimes treacherous. None of this prevents deep loyalty to family or to a true friend.

The Petty-dwarves — Noegyth Nibin Race is best suited to the First Age, and thereafter to rare survivors in later Ages. It should remain Restricted. The player should specify the location of the community, the number of survivors, the character's relationship with the Khazâd, distrust of Elves and the secret being protected.

He should not, however, be regarded as the moral model for his entire people.

A nearly extinct people

Even before their decline, their communities remained small and separate. By the Third Age, a group may consist of only a few related families, a single clan, several individuals living within a network of caves, or scattered survivors unaware that others still exist. This rarity explains their extreme secrecy: revealing the location of a dwelling could doom the whole community.

Gathering and knowledge of nature

Petty-dwarves possess less skill in smithing and masonry than the great Houses, but are much better at herbcraft, gathering and knowledge of the natural world. They recognise edible plants, nourishing roots, medicinal herbs, poisons, fungi, animal tracks, seasonal changes and natural shelters. Their relationship with nature is more utilitarian than that of the Elves, but can become deeply respectful.

Society, property and family

Their society is founded on family and the immediate survival of the group. Possession plays a central role: every tool, store and hiding place may determine everyone's survival. Marriage is monogamous and lasts for life; children are exceedingly precious because of the low population. They learn very early to remain silent, recognise plants, hide tracks, never reveal the dwelling and memorise escape routes.

A morality shaped by persecution

Ancient accounts describe them as quiet, possessive, greedy, suspicious and sometimes treacherous. For a more nuanced portrayal, these traits should be understood as consequences of a long history of persecution: silence protects dwellings, possessiveness protects scarce resources, cunning compensates for lack of numbers, and an agreement imposed under threat is not regarded as legitimate. None of this prevents deep loyalty to family or to a true friend.

Place in character creation

The Petty-dwarves — Noegyth Nibin Race is best suited to the First Age, and thereafter to rare survivors in later Ages. It should remain Restricted. The player should specify the location of the community, the number of survivors, the character's relationship with the Khazâd, distrust of Elves and the secret being protected.

Les Petits-Nains, appelés Noegyth Nibin en sindarin, forment une branche ancienne, déchue et presque éteinte des Khazâd. Bien avant le lever du Soleil et de la Lune, ils vivaient déjà dans des demeures secrètes et dispersées. Mîm est leur représentant le plus célèbre, mais quelques familles auraient survécu à la submersion du Beleriand.

Ils ne sont ni une Race entièrement étrangère aux Khazâd ni une simple Culture régionale. Leur longue séparation, les persécutions, l’endogamie et les privations ont transformé leur apparence et leur mode de vie.

Origines et exil

Ils descendraient d’un groupe de bannis de Nogrod, exilé après un meurtre. L’éloignement des grandes Maisons entraîna la perte de traditions artisanales, l’isolement des familles, une défiance croissante et une adaptation à une existence clandestine fondée sur la cueillette, les herbes et la dissimulation.

Les premiers habitants du Beleriand

Ils occupèrent plusieurs régions du Beleriand avant l’arrivée des Elfes. Certains furent chassés, traqués ou tués, ce qui nourrit leur haine durable envers les Elfes, particulièrement les Noldor. Leur mémoire conserve le souvenir de cavernes confisquées, de familles disparues et de terres perdues.

Amon Rûdh et Mîm

Mîm vivait avec ses fils dans les cavernes d’Amon Rûdh. Son histoire illustre leur attachement farouche au foyer, leur haine des Orcs, leur ressentiment envers les Elfes et leur volonté de survivre. Il ne doit toutefois pas être considéré comme le modèle moral de tout son peuple.

Un peuple presque éteint

Leurs communautés ne comptent souvent que quelques familles, un unique clan ou plusieurs survivants vivant dans un réseau de cavernes. Révéler l’emplacement d’une demeure pourrait condamner tout le groupe, ce qui explique leur secret extrême.

Apparence

Ils mesurent généralement entre 90 cm et 1,20 m. Leur peau va du brun sombre au gris, leur teint est souvent rougeaud, leurs membres noueux, leur tête large, leurs épaules courbées et leur barbe fine, broussailleuse et rarement entretenue.

Leur apparence peut être expliquée par la malnutrition, les conditions de vie difficiles et l’adaptation aux passages étroits, plutôt que par une corruption morale inhérente.

Longévité et endurance

Ils vivent généralement entre 250 et 400 ans. Malgré leur petite taille et leur posture voûtée, ils possèdent une endurance remarquable, adaptée aux déplacements souterrains, aux marches nocturnes, au transport de provisions et aux périodes de rationnement.

Résistances et vision

Comme les autres Khazâd, ils résistent bien au feu et au froid. Ils voient très bien dans la pénombre et sont parfaitement adaptés aux cavernes, tunnels, ruines et forêts nocturnes.

Furtivité

Leur petite taille et leur longue habitude de la clandestinité en font d’excellents infiltrateurs. Ils apprennent à marcher sans bruit, cacher une entrée, effacer des traces, se glisser dans des passages étroits, observer sans être vus et créer de fausses pistes.

Demeures cachées

Ils vivent dans des habitats creusés dans les collines, falaises ou affleurements rocheux. Une demeure comprend généralement une entrée dissimulée, des couloirs sinueux, une salle commune, quelques cellules familiales, un garde-manger, un atelier, une petite forge et plusieurs galeries de fuite.

Cueillette et nature

Moins compétents que les grandes Maisons dans les arts de la forge et de la maçonnerie, ils sont meilleurs dans l’usage des herbes, des racines, des champignons, des poisons et des ressources forestières. Leur rapport à la nature est utilitaire mais souvent respectueux, car une forêt généreuse assure la survie du clan.

Artisanat

Ils pratiquent forge simple, coutellerie, petite orfèvrerie, empennage, pièges, taille de pierre, bois, cuir et préparation d’herbes. Leurs objets paraissent souvent grossiers mais peuvent cacher mécanismes ingénieux, caches, lames escamotables ou poisons.

Vêtements

Ils portent des vêtements sombres et épais : capuches couvrant le visage, lourdes capes, bottes de cuir, pourpoints et pantalons ajustés. Les objets précieux sont dissimulés sous les vêtements ou cachés dans les demeures.

Religion

Ils révèrent Aulë sous une forme isolée de son nom et honorent aussi Yavanna, car les plantes et la forêt sont essentielles à leur survie. Leurs rites associent pierre, métal, cavernes, subsistance, mémoire des ancêtres et protection des familles.

Langues

Ils parlent surtout le westron et parfois le sindarin à l’extérieur. Entre eux, ils utilisent une forme archaïque et particulière du khuzdul, riche en termes liés aux anciennes demeures et à la forêt.

Relations

Ils utilisent cimeterres, dagues, arbalètes, frondes, épées courtes, hachettes, marteaux, lances et javelots. Le cuir souple et la maille ample sont courants.

Ils combattent par pièges, embuscades, tirs d’arbalète, fausses retraites, galeries de fuite, herbes et poisons. Dans leur propre demeure, chaque passage peut devenir une arme.

Petty-dwarves — Noegyth Nibin

The Petty-dwarves, called Noegyth Nibin in Sindarin, form an ancient, fallen and nearly extinct branch of the Khazâd. Long before the rising of the Sun and Moon, they already lived in secret and scattered dwellings. Mîm is their most famous representative, but a few families may have survived the drowning of Beleriand.

They are neither a Race entirely separate from the Khazâd nor merely a regional Culture. Their long separation, persecution, inbreeding and deprivation transformed both their appearance and way of life.

Origins and exile

They are said to descend from a group of exiles from Nogrod, banished after a murder. Separation from the great Houses led to the loss of craft traditions, the isolation of families, growing distrust and adaptation to a clandestine existence based on gathering, herbs and concealment.

The first inhabitants of Beleriand

They occupied several regions of Beleriand before the arrival of the Elves. Some were driven out, hunted or killed, feeding their lasting hatred of the Elves, especially the Noldor. Their memory preserves the loss of caves, vanished families and stolen lands.

Amon Rûdh and Mîm

Mîm lived with his sons in the caves of Amon Rûdh. His story illustrates their fierce attachment to home, hatred of Orcs, resentment toward Elves and determination to survive. He should not, however, be regarded as the moral model for his entire people.

A nearly extinct people

Their communities often consist of only a few families, a single clan or several survivors living within a network of caves. Revealing the location of a dwelling could doom the entire group, explaining their extreme secrecy.

Appearance

They generally stand between 90 cm and 1.20 m tall. Their skin ranges from dark brown to grey, their complexion is often ruddy, their limbs knotted, their heads broad, shoulders hunched and beards thin, bushy and seldom groomed.

Their appearance can be explained by malnutrition, harsh living conditions and adaptation to narrow passages rather than by any inherent moral corruption.

Longevity and endurance

They generally live between 250 and 400 years. Despite their small stature and stooped posture, they possess remarkable endurance suited to underground travel, night marches, carrying provisions and periods of rationing.

Resistances and vision

Like other Khazâd, they resist fire and cold well. They see very well in dim light and are perfectly adapted to caverns, tunnels, ruins and forests by night.

Stealth

Their small size and long habit of clandestine life make them excellent infiltrators. They learn to walk silently, conceal an entrance, erase tracks, slip through narrow passages, observe without being seen and lay false trails.

Hidden dwellings

They live in homes dug into hills, cliffs or rocky outcrops. A dwelling usually includes a concealed entrance, winding corridors, a common room, a few family cells, a pantry, a workshop, a small forge and several escape tunnels.

Gathering and nature

Less skilled than the great Houses in smithcraft and masonry, they are better at the use of herbs, roots, fungi, poisons and woodland resources. Their relationship with nature is practical but often respectful, because a generous forest ensures the clan's survival.

Craftsmanship

They practise simple smithing, knifemaking, minor jewellery, fletching, trapmaking, stonework, woodworking, leatherwork and herbal preparation. Their objects often appear crude but may conceal ingenious mechanisms, hidden compartments, retractable blades or poisons.

Clothing

They wear dark, heavy clothing: hoods covering the face, thick cloaks, leather boots, fitted doublets and trousers. Precious objects are concealed beneath clothing or hidden in their dwellings.

Society and family

Their society is founded on family and immediate survival. Authority belongs to the eldest, the owner of the dwelling, the best hunter or the most skilled craftsman. Marriage is monogamous, and children are exceedingly precious because of their low population.

Temperament

They are quiet, possessive, suspicious and cunning. These traits should be understood as consequences of a long history of persecution. They can be loyal to family, grateful to a true friend and generous when they do not feel threatened.

Religion

They revere Aulë under an isolated form of his name and also honour Yavanna, for plants and forests are essential to their survival. Their rites combine stone, metal, caverns, subsistence, remembrance of ancestors and the protection of families.

Languages

Outside their homes they chiefly speak Westron and sometimes Sindarin. Among themselves they use an archaic and distinctive form of Khuzdul, rich in terms connected with ancient dwellings and the forest.

Relations

Their relations with the Khazâd are complex: kinship is acknowledged, but so is the memory of exile. They particularly hate Elves, especially the Noldor, and also fight Orcs, Wargs, Trolls, brigands and underground monsters.

Weapons, armour and combat

They use scimitars, daggers, crossbows, slings, short swords, hatchets, hammers, spears and javelins. Supple leather and loose mail are common.

They fight through traps, ambushes, crossbow fire, feigned retreats, escape tunnels, herbs and poisons. Within their own dwelling, every passage can become a weapon.

Magic and professions

Rare Mages exist among them, but several magical and mental paths remain forbidden. They do not develop the disciplined military tradition of the great Houses; their fighters are more often hunters, rogues, guardians or scouts.

Amon Rûdh and Mîm

Mîm, the most famous of the Petty-dwarves, lived with his sons in the caves of Amon Rûdh. For a time his dwelling became a refuge for Túrin and his companions. His story illustrates fierce attachment to home, hatred of Orcs, resentment toward Elves, memory of humiliations and determination to preserve the last members of his family. He should not, however, be regarded as the moral model for his entire people.

A nearly extinct people

Even before their decline, their communities remained small and separate. By the Third Age, a group may consist of only a few related families, a single clan, several individuals living within a network of caves, or scattered survivors unaware that others still exist. This rarity explains their extreme secrecy: revealing the location of a dwelling could doom the whole community.

Gathering and knowledge of nature

Petty-dwarves possess less skill in smithing and masonry than the great Houses, but are much better at herbcraft, gathering and knowledge of the natural world. They recognise edible plants, nourishing roots, medicinal herbs, poisons, fungi, animal tracks, seasonal changes and natural shelters. Their relationship with nature is more utilitarian than that of the Elves, but can become deeply respectful.

Society, property and family

Their society is founded on family and the immediate survival of the group. Possession plays a central role: every tool, store and hiding place may determine everyone's survival. Marriage is monogamous and lasts for life; children are exceedingly precious because of the low population. They learn very early to remain silent, recognise plants, hide tracks, never reveal the dwelling and memorise escape routes.

A morality shaped by persecution

Ancient accounts describe them as quiet, possessive, greedy, suspicious and sometimes treacherous. For a more nuanced portrayal, these traits should be understood as consequences of a long history of persecution: silence protects dwellings, possessiveness protects scarce resources, cunning compensates for lack of numbers, and an agreement imposed under threat is not regarded as legitimate. None of this prevents deep loyalty to family or to a true friend.

Place in character creation

The Petty-dwarves — Noegyth Nibin Race is best suited to the First Age, and thereafter to rare survivors in later Ages. It should remain Restricted. The player should specify the location of the community, the number of survivors, the character's relationship with the Khazâd, distrust of Elves and the secret being protected.
